passage: One evening after dinner in their fourth-floor flat in Lisbon, Rosa's parents switched off the television. "Fire practice," said her father. Each child started in their own bedroom and traced the way to the stairs with a hand along the wall. Then they dropped to hands and knees and crawled low under an imaginary cloud of smoke. At every door they held the back of a hand near it before opening. "Not the lift," Mum reminded them. At the stairwell Rosa and her sister Ada counted the steps down to the street door together: sixty-two. Rosa was out of breath from laughing, and now she could find the way with her eyes shut.

qa.q: What did the children do at every door?
qa.a: They held the back of a hand near it before opening.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling at the end of the practice?
qa.a: Cheerful and confident, since she was laughing and could now find the way with her eyes shut.

qa.q: What could the family add to the practice, and why?
qa.a: They could agree on a place to meet outside and try the route once in the dark, so it feels closer to a real night.

qa.q: How might Ada have seen the practice?
qa.a: Ada probably found it partly a game, but by counting the steps with Rosa Ada also learned the way down.

grounding: A family walks each bedroom's route to the stairs and the children practise crawling low and checking doors.

passage: Abhinav's family lived in the warden's flat inside the boarding school, above the junior dormitory. On Tuesday evening, after the fire-safety week notice, his mother, Pallavi, said, "Tonight we practise." They started in Abhinav's room. "If there's smoke, crawl. Smoke rises, clean air stays low." Abhinav and his little brother crawled along the corridor on their hands and knees, giggling at first. At each door, Pallavi made them stop and touch it with the back of their hand. "If it's hot, don't open it. Go the other way." They traced the route from every bedroom to the stairs, not the lift, and out to the playground. They did it twice more, without the giggling.

qa.a: In the warden's flat inside the boarding school, above the junior dormitory.

qa.q: How did the boys feel on the first crawl compared with the later ones?
qa.a: At first they were amused and giggled, but by the later rounds they were serious and determined.

qa.q: What else could the family add to the practice, and why?
qa.a: They could agree a meeting spot outside and practise at night, because a real fire might happen in the dark.

qa.q: How does the drill look to Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi sees her sons learning the route properly and is probably reassured once the giggling stops.

grounding: It shows a family walking the escape route from each bedroom to the stairs, with the children practising crawling low and feeling doors.

passage: From our balcony opposite, on Sunday evening, I watched the Singh family do something strange. First the father, Sachin, walked slowly from every bedroom to the front door, counting steps. Then Jasleen and her little brother came out behind him on their hands and knees, crawling along the corridor. At each door they stopped, touched it with the back of a hand, then went on. They did it three times. The third time they went out to the stairs, not the lift. I didn't know what it was until Jasleen shouted, "Papa, forty seconds!" I couldn't tell if the children were scared or just enjoying it, but they looked very serious by the end.

qa.q: How long did Jasleen say the third round took?
What might Jasleen have been feeling by the end of the drill?
qa.a: She may have felt proud and focused, though the neighbour can't be sure whether she was scared or enjoying it.

qa.q: What else could the family practise, and why?
qa.a: They could practise at night with the lights off, because smoke and darkness make a real escape harder.

qa.q: How does the drill look to the neighbour watching?
qa.a: The neighbour is puzzled at first, then realises it is a safety practice, and is curious and a little impressed.

grounding: It shows a family rehearsing the escape route from each bedroom, with the children crawling low and feeling doors before opening them.
